cards.tip: FIX — When the customer mentioned getting a third opinion, you should have directly asked 'Which of these three options would you like to move forward with?' — getting them to commit to one option secures the decision before comparison shopping with other companies.

FIX — Customer proactively asked about maintenance, showing interest, but you need to present your repair or upgrade options first; run your full inspection and show 4-plus priced options during the diagnosis before taking the membership order.

WIN — When your customer asked if the membership meant you'd come check other things, you'd already shown 'it's a no-brainer': $312 in repair discounts against $192 annual membership cost—they went from hesitant to 'Yeah, why not?' because the numbers justified it.

FIX — When the customer mentioned the thermostat fan had been running continuously for 2 years, that was your opening to recommend a full system inspection or preventive maintenance package while you were already there—instead, you quickly adjusted the setting and moved on without exploring upgrade opportunities.

WIN — When Xavier presented the side-by-side cost comparison ($240 with membership and 15% future discounts versus $303 for just the part), the customer did the math and recognized the membership would pay for itself — they committed to the SAM signup.

FIX — When the customer expressed doubt about not getting a supervisor after two previous visits, that was the moment to reassure them and set clear expectations for what would make today different; the vague response didn't rebuild confidence.

WIN — Your clear diagnosis ('the wire is totally crisp...it probably could have been rubbed through and caused it to heat up') gave the customer confidence to approve the $264 repair immediately; when they said 'you're already here,' they signaled trust in your assessment.

FIX — When the customer said 'as long as we can just sleep tonight,' expressing worry about the new AC, you replied 'It hopefully should' instead of presenting 4+ options with pricing and offering the maintenance agreement—that conversation window is where the sale closes.

FIX — The customer confirmed systems were running normally with no complaints, which should have triggered the membership pitch and maintenance discussion; once the inspection confirms everything's working, circle back before leaving—'Your systems are running great and here's how we keep them that way with our SAM agreement'—even a maintenance call is a sales opportunity when you bring value through prevention, not just repair.

FIX — After the customer showed you the condensate line gunk and explained they'd cleaned it, that was your moment to say 'Good catch—once I finish inspecting, I'll show you a couple ways we can prevent that buildup and keep your system running efficiently'—that plants the seed for maintenance options before you present pricing.

FIX — After confirming the system's working well, present 4–6 repair/upgrade options with pricing, then ask for approval to proceed—you stopped after diagnosis and got into internal equipment talk instead of building the customer's menu to choose from.

WIN — After the successful test, you asked 'all I need from you now is $112—do you want to use one of the cards on file, or—' and the customer immediately agreed and paid; a direct ask right after proving the system works is your repeatable close for service calls.

FIX — Customer didn't object to your prices on the Vegas kit and switch replacement, but you jumped to email confirmation without asking 'Should I go ahead with both of these?'—get that approval before you leave.

FIX — When the customer indicated the system is loud, you started investigating with 'Is that your air filter?'—complete that diagnosis by explaining the cause, present 2-3 specific options with pricing (filter upgrade, coil cleaning, efficiency upgrade), and ask directly which solution works best for them.

FIX — After your clear capacitor diagnosis, the customer was ready to commit—instead of one $264 quote, say 'We can do the capacitor for $264 alone, or add our maintenance plan to prevent this again'—presenting options up front gets the yes before the landlord objection.

WIN — Customer expressed concern about being caught without AC in 107-degree heat and having to pay for a hotel during emergency repair. Tech reframed the upgrade as preventive: 'That's why we offer stuff like this, so we can try to avoid things like that.' Tech validated the customer's own logic rather than pushing, letting the customer reach the conclusion to buy.

FIX — Customer described ongoing temperature balance issues; you checked the system and found it in spec, but never presented upgrade options (maintenance membership, zoning adjustment) or asked for their business—missing the chance to close a sale or at minimum get clear approval to proceed.

FIX — When the customer said 'you're the professional, I don't know what options I need'—step in with 2–3 clear scenarios (minimal/recommended/comprehensive) and ask directly 'which one works best to get you to 100% today?'—that advisory close would have locked it down instead of it floating on a pending email.

FIX — When the customer signaled affordability constraints ('if we can afford it now'), ask what they CAN afford today and build a solution at that price point—Matthew presented one option and scheduled for later, leaving the real objection unresolved.

WIN — She said she'd been charged at the old house and wouldn't sign anything else; you went to your boss and came back with 'I told him and he's putting a note on your account'—that ownership took her from walking away to signed membership.

FIX — After your evaluation, you went straight to technical voltage and wiring details instead of circling back with distinct repair options and pricing—customers need to see choices first, so they know what to approve and what it costs.

FIX — When the customer confirmed understanding of the switch issue ('it's probably the one that's tied to these 2 thermostats?'), that was your moment to convert: 'Since you have less than a year on warranty and this switch is showing failure signs, I'd recommend we replace it now for [price] to avoid a no-cool emergency — shall we get that scheduled?' Instead you said 'something to think about,' and the customer left without approving either repair.

FIX — When customers heard about the voltage switch corrosion and high amperage issues, they were engaged but Juan said 'I just don't want the next tech to come and be like, hey, did they ever bring this up to your attention?' instead of presenting a structured menu of 4+ options with pricing and asking directly 'Which option works for you?'—missing both the options presentation and the close.

FIX — When the customer asked 'How much is that gonna be?' and then said 'let me talk to my wife about it,' you needed to test that buying signal ('Does $1,877 work for your budget?') and then ask directly: 'Perfect—let me get you scheduled for [date], so once you two decide we can get started right away,' instead of leaving it to them to call back.

FIX — When the customer said 'everything's going okay' but both units weren't working, you clarified the problem but missed framing the visit. When you said 'I'm just gonna run my thorough evaluation, figuring out what's going on,' set expectations instead: 'I'll diagnose both systems, show you what I find, and walk you through your options to get this running again. Should take about an hour.' That frame gives customers confidence to approve work and upgrades later.

WIN — When the customer expressed frustration about upstairs cooling issues, you discovered the root cause in the attic and explained it clearly: 'You have a duct that just fell off...it ain't going where it's supposed to be going.' This clarity, backed by photo evidence, transformed the repair from optional to necessary, and the customer immediately approved both the $388 repair and SAM membership.

WIN — Your consequence-driven explanation won the motor start sale. You said 'Your battery's run out of juice... Your compressor is going to start overheating and then it's going to break down your compressor. That's like a four grand change out.' The customer understood that the $474 repair was insurance against a $4,000 compressor failure. When you offered to do it today, the customer closed on himself: 'So let's do the motor start thing.' Lead with the consequence of NOT fixing it, and the customer will ask you to do the work.

WIN — When the customer mentioned the fan running every hour, Stanley immediately identified the root cause, switched it to auto mode, and clearly explained the result; the instant problem-solving earned the customer's confidence and their signature.

FIX — when the customer confirms the problem is active (cycling, warm air at wrong temperature), present the three options (motor device replacement, full unit upgrade, maintenance membership) and pricing right then — waiting until later means the customer's already decided to think about it and you lose the sale to a competitor.

FIX — When customer expressed interest in the air cabinet but said he'd discuss it with his wife, you said 'I'll call Monday'—instead, ask what's really in the way ('cost or her input?'), then lock it in now: 'Details tonight, 6 PM tomorrow with both of you—let's schedule it.' That move—clarifying the objection then committing to a specific time—is where deals close.

FIX — When the customer acknowledged the discolored voltage switch, you said 'I would recommend that in the springtime' instead of asking 'Would you like to go ahead with that replacement today?'—the customer was on-site, knew the issue from your last visit, and was ready; that's where you close.

FIX — When the customer mentioned she does filters quarterly and keeps spares on hand, that's your moment to pitch SAM membership ('we handle all your filter changes, priority scheduling, and typically save you money')—offer the plan instead of just switching them out as a courtesy.

WIN — You showed the dust buildup with a photo, explained how it damages the motor, offered options from $400 cleaning to $3,000 cabinet, and when they chose the $180 filter, you closed immediately with a price quote and signature request—no hesitation, no second-guessing. That's what sealed the deal.

WIN — Your member discount pitch closed this one—when you said 'the $1,351 with member savings from the $1,590,' the customer saw the value and signed; next time, lead with 2-3 price tiers so they're choosing from options, not just hearing one recommendation.

FIX — When your customer said he'd talk to his son, instead of accepting the deferral, ask 'What's his main concern—cost, timeline, or repair versus replace?' and offer 'I can walk you through those now if you want to call him'—stay in the conversation instead of handing off quotes.
WIN — After replacing the motor start device, Tyler reported "Yeah, she's running," which gave the customer immediate proof that the diagnosis was right and justified the $447 cost.

FIX — When the customer asked about cost, you left to write the estimate without first giving a quick verbal options sketch ('soft-start-only at $X or the full package at $Y') and a timeline—instead keep them engaged by saying 'I'll have you those options in about 10 minutes' so you don't lose momentum.

FIX — When the customer signaled the soft start was the right upgrade to protect their new compressor, you should've asked: "Let me get that $1,380 soft start installed for you today" — instead you pivoted to other components and never circled back to close the sale.

WIN — You sealed the membership close by connecting diagnosis to immediate action: after showing the failed capacitor, you asked 'If you guys sign up on the membership today, I can definitely do that summer maintenance... I'll clean up, I'll open it up, test everything on the both units'—giving the customer who'd wanted to join before a concrete reason to stop deferring and act now.

FIX — Jose gave the right recommendation ($1,351 compressor repair) when the customer asked 'which one do you recommend?', but he didn't ask to schedule it; a direct close ('Should we get that scheduled this week?') would have either locked the sale or surfaced the real barrier so Jose could offer financing.

FIX — When the customer expressed budget concerns about filters, you should have pivoted to ask 'What else have you noticed about the system?' and built a tiered good/better/best options menu instead of staying in filter-price negotiation alone.

WIN — You explained the findings clearly ('didn't hit the pipe, looks good'), took photos to document it, and your direct 'How would you like to pay?' got an immediate card tap—straightforward close after solid diagnosis builds trust.

FIX — When you confirmed the pan was level and draining properly, you should have offered the membership agreement to prevent this on all his properties instead of just approving their work and leaving.

FIX — when the customer mentioned the thermostat keeps disconnecting from the app, acknowledge it's a known issue then propose an upgrade: 'I can get you a couple of options for a thermostat that'll connect reliably every time' and ask for the sale—instead you just said you've heard bad things about that app and moved on.

WIN — Adrian confidently communicated 'everything's checking out good' with 'no real concerns,' then directly asked to 'collect your signature' and the customer approved the $39 tune-up without hesitation.
WIN — Finding and fixing both the capacitors and thermostat with clear options and live proof (84° to 60° temp split) won you not just this job, but got them to ditch the other quote.

WIN — Your diagnosis of the batch defect and two-step solution plan ('I'm going to put a new one on there for right now... put in an order to get a stock standard OEM Lennox one') turned the customer's frustration with repeated failures into approval to move forward.

FIX — When the second homeowner woke up upset about the unannounced visit, you should have offered to do a quick 20-minute coil wash right then to show the value of the maintenance agreement, instead of immediately offering to reschedule, which lost the work for that day.

FIX — When the customer said they didn't have budget for major repairs, Jose backed off instead of walking through 3–4 tiered repair options with specific pricing—letting the customer choose what they could afford and get work approved.

WIN — When Jack hit the moment where he needed the customer to understand why a capacitor was worth replacing, he said 'Think of it like a car battery for your alternator'—that analogy cut through the technical jargon and made them comfortable enough to approve the repair right away.

FIX — You had the customer ready when you said you'd fix it today, but you never quoted pricing or presented repair options for the actuator before pivoting to the membership; come back with a specific repair quote (standard vs. upgraded actuator), close that first, then layer in the membership.

WIN — You explained the root cause in customer-friendly language ('there's a trap...if that secondary one dries out, it flaps around making that noise'), which built instant trust in your diagnosis, and then you asked directly for the business and closed it.

WIN — You showed up prepared with the replacement part and set clear time expectations upfront ('it'll take 5 minutes. No problem.'), which kept the customer confident and got the job closed smoothly.

WIN — When the customer objected that $430 was too expensive, you escalated to the manager and discovered the 10-year warranty that cut the cost to $224 labor-only. "So we are able to change that part under your guys's warranty. All we would be paying today would be just be, uh, the labor. It would go down to $224 rather than the $430." She signed on the spot.

WIN — When the wife hesitated on cost, you showed her the actual burnt contactor and explained, 'if it does go out the outdoor fan won't come on and the compressor won't come on so it won't blow any cold air' — making the failure scenario real instead of hypothetical, which got her to approve the $426 repair instead of deferring it.

FIX — After catching that disconnected drain line (an installation defect that could've caused water damage), you had the perfect setup to pitch the membership: 'That's exactly why we recommend preventive maintenance—two check-ups a year to catch issues like this before they become costly problems. For you, splitting time between Nevada and Utah, it's peace of mind.' You proved your value; you just needed to ask for the sale.

FIX — When the customer worried about the unit dying in 10 hours, your response was vague; you should've said 'Let me check the transformer first since that's what Pedro worked on' to show a specific diagnostic plan.

FIX — When Robert said 'keep it as low to no cost as possible,' Corey should have reframed it with 'I'll do a complimentary inspection and show you exactly what I find — then if there are upgrades worth considering, I'll walk you through options and pricing' instead of just accepting the low-cost frame without opening the door to options.

FIX — When the customer said 'I like all your recommendations,' you backed off with 'totally fine' instead of moving to close; rephrase to 'Perfect! The switch and turbo starter are the critical ones—which do we start with this week?' to convert her approval into a direct ask for the business.

FIX — Customer said 'I feel like it's a little dangerous to do nothing'—that was the moment to ask directly 'Can I write up the leak check for you today?'—instead the call drifted and you never locked in approval for Sierra's service.
